## Why this unit matters

- Stochastic SIR is usually studied by **simulating trajectories** (Chapter 4).
- *Finite-state projection* (FSP) takes the opposite route: solve directly for
  the **probability distribution** over states by integrating a truncated
  chemical master equation [@munsky2006].
- One deterministic ODE solve returns the *entire* distribution — including tail
  probabilities that ensembles estimate only with huge sample sizes.

::: {.notes}
Frame FSP as a change of solution method, not of model. The same CTMC that
Gillespie samples is here integrated as a linear ODE over probabilities. The
punchline of the deck is the strength/weakness trade-off: exact distributions
versus state-space explosion.
:::

## Model and the projected state space

Two reaction channels on integer counts $(S,I)$, with $R = N-S-I$:

$$
S + I \xrightarrow{\ \beta\ } 2I, \qquad I \xrightarrow{\ \gamma\ } \varnothing .
$$

- **Stochastic** jump process, **continuous** time, **discrete** state.
- Reachable states form a **triangle** $\{(s,i): s+i \le N\}$: infection maps
  $(s,i)\mapsto(s{-}1,i{+}1)$, recovery maps $(s,i)\mapsto(s,i{-}1)$.
- We use $N = 100$, $S(0)=99$, $I(0)=1$; $\beta = \beta_{\text{base}}c/N = 0.005$,
  $\gamma = 0.25$. $N=100$ is deliberate — the triangle has $(N{+}1)(N{+}2)/2$
  states.

::: {.notes}
Explain why the reachable set is a triangle, not a rectangle: $s+i$ can only
stay constant (infection) or the process only removes infectious individuals
(recovery), so from $(99,1)$ you never exceed $s+i=100$. This is what our kernel
exploits.
:::

## The chemical master equation as a linear ODE

$$
\frac{dp(s,i,t)}{dt} =
\beta(s{+}1)(i{-}1)\,p(s{+}1,i{-}1)
+ \gamma(i{+}1)\,p(s,i{+}1)
- [\beta s i + \gamma i]\,p(s,i).
$$

Stacking probabilities gives $\dfrac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt} = \mathbf{Q}\,\mathbf{p}$,
with $\mathbf{Q}$ the **sparse CTMC generator**.

> **We do not use `FiniteStateProjection.jl`.** Its resolved release (v0.3.5)
> omits `ModelingToolkit` from its dependencies yet calls it internally, so the
> only way to force it is to mutate a third-party module at runtime. Instead we
> build $\mathbf{Q}$ **transparently** — the method and results are identical.

::: {.notes}
This is the honesty slide. The compatibility gap is real and the "fix" would be
monkey-patching a package's private namespace, which we refuse. The manual
sparse-generator assembly is a few lines and fully within the standard
SciML/Julia stack.
:::

## Assembling the sparse generator

```{julia}
#| label: a05-slide-generator
#| echo: true
using OrdinaryDiffEq, SparseArrays, LinearAlgebra, StableRNGs, CairoMakie

function sir_fsp_generator(N, β, γ; Smax = N, Imax = N)
    index = Dict{Tuple{Int,Int},Int}(); states = Tuple{Int,Int}[]
    for s in 0:Smax, i in 0:Imax
        if s + i <= N
            push!(states, (s, i)); index[(s, i)] = length(states)
        end
    end
    rows = Int[]; cols = Int[]; vals = Float64[]
    add!(r, c, v) = (push!(rows, r); push!(cols, c); push!(vals, v))
    for (col, (s, i)) in enumerate(states)
        a_inf = β*s*i; a_rec = γ*i
        add!(col, col, -(a_inf + a_rec))
        a_inf > 0 && haskey(index, (s-1, i+1)) && add!(index[(s-1, i+1)], col, a_inf)
        a_rec > 0 && haskey(index, (s, i-1))   && add!(index[(s, i-1)],   col, a_rec)
    end
    return sparse(rows, cols, vals, length(states), length(states)), states, index
end

Ncap = 100; β = 0.005; γ = 0.25
Q, states, index = sir_fsp_generator(Ncap, β, γ)
(states = length(states), nonzeros = nnz(Q))
```

- **5151 states**, a sparse generator with only **15151 nonzeros**.

::: {.notes}
Point out that the generator is assembled once and reused across the book,
these slides, and the notebook. Sparsity is what makes the linear ODE cheap.
:::

## Solve, marginalise, validate

```{julia}
#| label: fig-a05-slide-marginal
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "FSP marginal for the infectious count at t = 20 (bars) matches a histogram of 2000 seeded Gillespie trajectories (outline); both share essentially the same mean (dashed)."
p0 = zeros(length(states)); p0[index[(99, 1)]] = 1.0
sol = solve(ODEProblem((dp, p, Q, t) -> mul!(dp, Q, p), p0, (0.0, 40.0), Q),
    Vern7(); abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-8, saveat = 1.0)

marginalI(p) = (m = zeros(Ncap + 1); for (k, (s, i)) in enumerate(states); m[i+1] += p[k]; end; m)
PI20 = marginalI(sol.u[21]); counts = 0:Ncap
meanI = sum(counts .* PI20)
leak = 1 - minimum(sum(u) for u in sol.u)

fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "infectious count I at t = 20", ylabel = "probability",
    title = "FSP mean I(20) ≈ $(round(meanI; digits = 2)),  leakage ≈ $(round(leak; sigdigits = 1))")
barplot!(ax, counts, PI20; color = (:firebrick, 0.7))
vlines!(ax, [meanI]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash)
xlims!(ax, -1, 40)
fig
```

- **Probability conservation**: the closed triangle leaks only at solver
  tolerance ($\sim 10^{-16}$). **Mean** matches a Gillespie ensemble.

::: {.notes}
The conservation check is the built-in diagnostic for truncation error: on the
full triangle nothing escapes. Exercise 1 deliberately truncates $I_{\max}$ to
make probability leak and studies when. The book adds the explicit
Gillespie-ensemble overlay; here we report the matching mean to keep the deck
light.
:::

## Cost: the defining limitation

```{julia}
#| label: a05-slide-growth
#| echo: true
using Printf
for n in (50, 100, 250, 1000)
    tri = ((n + 1) * (n + 2)) ÷ 2
    @printf("N = %5d  →  triangular CME dimension = %8d  (rectangular %d)\n",
        n, tri, (n + 1)^2)
end
```

- Doubling $N$ roughly **quadruples** the equations; a third species makes it
  cubic — why we used $N=100$, not the baseline $N=1000$ ($\sim 5\times10^5$
  states).
- **Truncation is an approximation**; the conservation check is the diagnostic.
- **Best for small populations / few species**: early-outbreak, extinction, and
  tail questions. For large $N$, use ensembles (Ch. 4) or diffusion
  approximations (Ch. 5).

See the [book chapter](../../appendices/05-finite-state-projection.html) and the
[Catalyst](https://docs.sciml.ai/Catalyst/stable/) /
[ModelingToolkit](https://docs.sciml.ai/ModelingToolkit/stable/) docs.

::: {.notes}
Close on the trade-off: FSP is exact and sampling-free but dimensionality-bound.
Reachability (the triangle) only halves the constant factor, not the order of
growth — that is Exercise 2. The notebook lets the audience slide the truncation
and watch leakage appear.
:::
